inline.s: Answer: it is the one who knows observing. When deluded, the thinker is in charge; when awake, the one who knows is in charge. The heart of the path to liberation is simply to let the one who knows be in charge.
Question: what is the meaning of “Contemplate the thought and the thought abides; awaken to delusion and delusion is all true”?

Answer: these are words from an account of Chan practice in Master Tanxu’s autobiography, Recollections of Shadows and Dust: “At first, when I sat, deluded thoughts arose straightaway, like waves in the sea, one wave chasing the next, the next chasing the one after, never stopping; I could not suppress them, and I grew very anxious. Later I stopped suppressing them and instead used the power of contemplation to watch them, watching where a deluded thought actually arises from. Watched in this way, the deluded thought vanished; gone, it arose again, and arising, it was watched again. After a long time, the deluded thoughts gradually ceased to arise, and my mind became very tranquil and natural.”

Once, sitting the second evening stick of incense, I felt that scarcely had I crossed my legs when the closing bell rang; afterwards the man on the next cushion told me that a full long stick of incense had long since passed. During that stick of incense, though it seemed no great time had gone by, I felt body and mind most serene and in accord with the Dharma, with a kind of well-being beyond words; and unawares, from the ground of my nature, two lines welled up: ‘Contemplate the thought and the thought abides; awaken to delusion and delusion is all true.’ At first I did not dare to believe these two lines were right, so later I went and asked old Master Di (Master Dixian), and old Master Di gave his seal of approval.”

Contemplate the thought and the thought abides” means: when deluded thoughts keep arising, observe them attentively, and they come to a stop. “Awaken to delusion and delusion is all true” means: the deluded mind and the true mind are two states of the one mind; when you awaken to and illumine this mind of deluded thinking (the deluded mind), it turns into the true mind of no-thought.

Master Tanxu said: “Therefore, beginners in practice need not fear having deluded thoughts. When a deluded thought is present, watch it with the wisdom that can observe, and the deluded thought comes to a stop (this deluded thought is halted); at the same time, awaken to the fact that this deluded mind is the true mind—there is no true mind apart from the deluded mind, no separate true mind elsewhere.”

blocks.text: 3. Not Departing from the Present Thought

inline.s: Not departing from the present thought means that in walking, standing, sitting, and lying down, one does not depart from awareness of the present thought, and achieves awareness the moment a thought arises (the instant a deluded thought arises, one sees it at once). If a deluded thought arises, at once cry out a rebuke (for example, “Wrong!”) and cut it off, not letting it continue; if no deluded thought arises, simply watch in this way. Or again: if a deluded thought arises, with a single stern awakening, and in the very awakening it is gone. Or again: if a deluded thought arises, watch what it wants to think about, and the deluded thought subsides of itself. In sum, there are many particular methods for cutting off deluded thinking; each person adopts them according to his own situation. But one must achieve awareness the moment a thought arises and disappearance in the very awareness, until not a single thought arises.

Not departing from the present thought means being aware of the present thought at all times and in all places. To be aware of the present thought and enter the state of no-thought is to be free from appearances; this is to do the work of freedom from appearances at the very place where thought stirs and moves. Within, one is not turned about by thoughts; without, one is not dragged along by circumstances; amid the vast storm of circumstances, one remains in charge of oneself.
Freedom from appearances

] means not clinging to appearances—knowing that appearances are illusory, not being deluded by appearances, not being turned about by appearances. The Diamond Sutra says: “If you see all appearances as no appearances, you see the Tathagata.”

The skill of not departing from the present thought is extremely important; it is the basic training of both Chan investigation and Buddha-recitation. If deluded thoughts arise and you cannot even see them, if you are shrouded by deluded thoughts, how can you investigate Chan? How can you recite the Buddha’s name and attain single-mindedness? Therefore this skill must be practiced on the cushion and off it, practiced in walking, standing, sitting, and lying down, practiced throughout the twelve double hours of the day, practiced until it is utterly solid.

This stage of study is in fact a continuation and deepening of “knowing yet not following” in the previous section. From “knowing yet not following” one must go further and achieve “awareness the moment a thought arises, disappearance in the very awareness,” until not a single thought arises and movement and stillness are merged into one.

At this stage, if awareness is focused and continuous, deluded thoughts do not arise; with the slightest lapse, deluded thoughts arise. So one must maintain awareness at all times and work at “awareness the moment a thought arises”: the instant a deluded thought arises, be aware of it at once and do not let it continue. At all times one must check whether one has fallen into the world of the head (into idle thinking); if so, it means awareness has been lost and must immediately be raised again. Once awareness is raised, it is like the sun at high noon, and the demons and sprites hide away: deluded thoughts leave no trace or shadow, and the hard ice of habitual tendencies melts too. When you reach this point, you must place your attention on not losing awareness. When this becomes thoroughly familiar over a long time, you enter the state in which not a single thought arises. Reciting the Buddha’s name on this foundation, you will certainly attain single-mindedness, and can go on to cultivate the samādhi of Buddha-recitation.

The skill of not departing from the present thought must be practiced in two ways: one is to strengthen one’s own power of awareness, the other is to weaken the force with which sense-objects entangle one. The work of weakening the entangling force of sense-objects is done in the midst of daily life, at the place where thought stirs and moves, through seeing through and letting go. The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: “Knowing the illusion, one is at once free of it, without resort to any means; being free of the illusion, one is at once enlightened, and there are no stages.” The Vimalakirti Sutra says: “He is able to distinguish well all the marks of dharmas, yet in the ultimate meaning he does not move.” (He can clearly discern all dharmas, while his mind is not moved by these illusions.) On these matters there are detailed discussions in the teaching materials of the “Prajnā Smashing Delusion” stage of the Online Buddhist Academy of Practice According to the Teaching,
Pure Practice

, namely the Detailed Explanation of the Diamond Sutra, the Detailed Explanation of the Heart Sutra, the Detailed Explanation of the Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch, and Selected Annotations on the Sutra of the Buddha’s Treasury. One should constantly observe what it is that pulls you away from the present moment and plunges you into deluded thinking. You must find out the events and causes that pull you away from the present moment and apply the remedy to the disease, treating the serious first. Especially at critical moments, you must be able to forbear, and then be able to transform.

[Ultimate meaning] The supreme truth, that is, the true aspect of all dharmas. The Buddha said: “All dharmas are false and unreal; where they cease, that is called the real, is called the true aspect, is called the Dharma realm, is called ultimate wisdom, is called the ultimate truth, is called the emptiness of the ultimate meaning.” (Mahāparinirvāṇa Sutra,
Fascicle Forty,
Chapter on Kaundinya)

The principle on which those who recite the Buddha’s name view and handle worldly affairs is this: to turn away from the Saha world and seek the Pure Land with joy, to clear away every interference, and to attain single-mindedness. On these matters there are detailed discussions in the last two chapters of this book (“Turning Away from the Saha World” and “Right Mindfulness at the Time of Death”) and in the teaching materials of the “Returning to the Pure Land” stage of “Practice According to the Teaching” (Annotated Essential Explanation of the Amitabha Sutra, A Treatise on Buddha-Recitation, The Essentials of Chan and Pure Land, and A Detailed Explanation of In Search of the Elephant of Buddha-Recitation Samādhi). Master Lianchi said: “Seventy has always been rare, and of a hundred years how many can one live (seventy has been rare since ancient times; how many reach a hundred)? Now, in this evening scene of life, one should open one’s heart wide and see through the world as no more than a play—where in it is there anything real? Just use one recitation of Amitābha Buddha to while away the hours, and take the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss as your own home. If I recite the Buddha’s name now, later I shall be born in the West—what greater fortune could there be! Give rise to great joy, and do not breed affliction. Should you meet with something unwelcome, turn your mind around at once, quickly raise this one recitation of the Buddha, and reflect back: I am a person of Amitābha Buddha’s world—how could I stoop to the common measure of worldly people! Turn anger into joy and recite the Buddha’s name with one mind; this is the great peace and the great method of liberation for a person of wisdom.” (Dharma Collection of Yunqi)

In general, when sense-objects entangle you, it is a test of whether your faith and vows are genuine; every test is a struggle of life and death, and you must be clear in principle and thorough in practice (thorough in the actual doing), and with great perseverance and forbearance free yourself from the entanglement. Pass one test, and you have advanced one stage toward the Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss.

Not departing from the present thought is also the foundation for understanding the mind and seeing one’s nature. When awareness of the present thought is unbroken and you keep to no-thought (not a single thought arising), with movement and stillness merged into one, then within no-thought look into and perceive your original face. Master Hanshan said: “The tongs and hammer that old man Dahui habitually used were meant only to block off the flow of deluded thinking beneath the faculty of mind at the huatou, so that it does not go on; and there, where it does not go on, to look into and perceive your original face.” (Collected Works of Dream Wandering,
Instructions on the Essentials of Chan Investigation)

Master Hanshan also said: “Even now, in this dream of ignorance, how can one clear away old karma? One must use the light of wisdom to shine through ignorance, deeply believe that one’s own mind is originally pure, and not be driven about by deluded thoughts and inversion; then karmas have no cause, because deluded thinking is the cause of all karma. Why is this so? From beginningless time we have been deluded about our own original mind, and life after life we have created all kinds of karma with the mind of deluded thinking. The habitual seeds of karma accumulate within the eighth consciousness (the alaya consciousness), and are watered with the water of ignorance, so that these evil seeds send forth shoots of karma: this is the root of transgression, and from it all evil karma arises. Now, if old karma is to be cleared away, one must first arouse the great light of wisdom, shine through ignorance, and forbid deluded thinking to sprout and quietly grow. If, at the place where deluded thought arises, one cuts it off with a single thought, then the old accumulations at the root of karma are cleared away on the spot. As it is said: do not fear that a thought arises, only fear that awareness is late. If awareness and illumination are a little late, you are turned about by it. If in daily life, at the place where thought stirs and moves, you are aware of and extinguish each thought, this is what is called ‘all offenses are like frost and dew; the sun of wisdom can dissolve them.’ Since the darkness of ignorance is broken only by wisdom, it is said that wisdom can dissolve them. If (you) do not let up day or night, diligently observing and not letting it pass, but simply, at the very place where deluded thought arises, investigate it to the end until there is no mark of arising at all—looking and looking again, in the end it is nowhere to be found. When this is thoroughly familiar over a long time, your own mind is pure and without a thing, and the mind without things is the true aspect. If you constantly contemplate this mind, what deluded thought can find room in it, what accumulated karma can lodge there? … One must take awareness and illumination as the root of practice. … Without the light of wisdom, how can one break through the darkness of delusion? It is only necessary that awareness and illumination be unmisted, and when the light of wisdom appears before you, that is the time for ending karmic hindrance and escaping birth and death.” (Collected Works of Dream Wandering,
Instructions to Dong Zhiguang)

Master Hanshan also said: “What is called cultivation is simply following one’s own mind and purifying away the shadows of deluded thinking and habitual tendencies (deluded thinking and habitual tendencies are both illusory and unreal, hence they are called shadows). To apply effort here is what is called cultivation. If a single thought of deluded thinking suddenly ceases, and one thoroughly sees that one’s own mind is originally perfect, luminous, vast, pure by nature, utterly without a single thing, this is called awakening. … In doing the work nowadays, one must first cut away (“cut away” is the same as “shovel away”) intellectual understanding, and work precisely and solely on this one thought. Deeply believe that your own mind is originally utterly clean, not a thread hanging on it, perfectly round and bright, filling the Dharma realm. Originally there is no body or mind, no world, and no deluded thinking or emotional brooding. Even this one thought is itself unborn. All the various states before you are illusory and unreal; they are only shadows appearing in the true mind. Pierce through them in this way, and then, at the place where deluded thoughts arise and cease, fix your gaze on them with a single look. Watch them: from where do they arise, and where do they cease? Press in hard like this, and no matter what deluded thoughts come, one press shatters them, and on the spot they melt like ice and crumble like tiles. Never follow after them and turn about, and never let them continue; this is what Yongjia meant by “one must cut off the mind of continuation.” For the empty and floating mind has no root or thread at all, and one must never take it as a real thing and let it lie across the chest. When it arises, at once cry “Duo!” (
duō

, a shout of rebuke), and with one shout it vanishes. Never suppress it (never press the thought down), for then it will lead you about as it pleases (otherwise you will be turned around by it), like a gourd on the water (press this one down and that one floats up again). Just cast body, mind, and world to one side and single-mindedly raise this one thought. Like a sword sweeping across the sky, whether it be a Buddha or a demon, cut them all off at once, as one cuts through tangled silk. Press on with bare strength, and this is what is meant by the straightforward mind and right mindfulness of true suchness. Right mindfulness is no-thought. To be able to contemplate no-thought may be called turning toward the Buddha’s wisdom.” (Collected Works of Dream Wandering,
Reply to Vice Censor-in-Chief Zheng Kunyan)

blocks.text: Part Two: Reciting the Buddha’s Name

inline.s: Once the Buddha’s name is raised, deluded thoughts all vanish; the joy of it cannot be put into words.

Every one of our thoughts is either cultivating pure karma or creating the karma of rebirth. Right mindfulness is the mind turning karma; deluded thought is karma binding the mind. Therefore treasure every thought: be mindful of the Buddha alone, thought following thought without a break. Constantly check yourself: is this cultivating pure karma, or creating the karma of rebirth? Is the mind turning karma, or is karma binding the mind? If you are not reciting the Buddha’s name, reflect at once: why am I not reciting? And immediately raise the Buddha’s name. Let the mind not seek conditions outside; take one recitation of the Buddha’s name as your very life root, never forgetting from thought to thought, never breaking from mind to mind.

The state of being aware yet free of deluded thoughts is called clear awareness. The essential point of Buddha-recitation is to make clear awareness stand firm, stand long, join into one continuous piece, resist interference, and let one live within clear awareness. To be “free of deluded thoughts” means: either right mindfulness (the thought of reciting the Buddha) or no-thought without dullness.
Master Chewu, the twelfth patriarch of the Pure Land school, said in his “Eight Essentials of Pure Practice”:
One: to be truly intent on birth and death and to give rise to the bodhi mind—this is the common road of those who study the Way.
Two: to hold the Buddha’s name with deep faith and earnest vows—this is the orthodox practice of the Pure Land.
Three: to recite by gathering in the mind and focusing it—this is the first expedient means.
Four: to break and subdue the afflictions presently at work—this is the essential task of cultivating the mind.
Five: to firmly uphold the four grave precepts—this is the root of entering the Way.
Six: to take various ascetic practices as aids to cultivating the Way.
Seven: to take single-mindedness as the home of the purified mind.
Eight: to take various auspicious signs as proof of rebirth in the Pure Land.
These eight matters should each be earnestly explained; those who cultivate pure karma cannot afford not to know them.

[Four grave precepts] The precepts against killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and lying. Killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and lying are natural offenses; their nature is evil, and one incurs the retribution of transgression whether or not the Buddha has laid down a rule against them.
Master Ciyun, the Repentance Master, said:

“For those who recite the Buddha’s name there are six surpassing benefits. First, all Buddhas and bodhisattvas protect and remember them, Amitābha dwells above their heads and sends forth light, and the gods and heavenly generals secretly aid them day and night. Second, evil ghosts and poisons cannot harm them, and the three disasters and eight adversities are all dissolved. Third, past hindrances are clear as ice and their karmic creditors are released. Fourth, their strength is full and no untimely illness befalls them. Fifth, they sleep and dream auspiciously, see the Buddha’s bodily form, and no nonhuman beings steal away their vital essence. Sixth, in this life they are reverenced by all, and at the end the three sages come to receive them. Thus one knows that reciting the Buddha’s name once in daily life is to prepare the Dharma for the unforeseen. It is like a person going into the city on business, who must first find lodging: when evening falls and it grows dark, he has a place to put up. To seek lodging beforehand is to cultivate pure karma in advance. For evening to fall and darkness to come is the arrival of the final limit. To have a place to put up is to be born within a lotus flower and meet no hindrance or difficulty. If a person applies his mind in this way, at the end he will surely attain rebirth.”
(Commentary and Notes on the Perfect Penetration Chapter of Great Strength Bodhisattva)

[Master Ciyun, the Repentance Master] Master Zunshi of the Song dynasty, whose epithet was Ciyun; he established the repentance ritual for rebirth in the Pure Land, the repentance ritual for invoking Guanyin to dispel poison and harm, the Golden Light Repentance, and other such rites, and so later generations called him “Master Ciyun, the Repentance Master.” [Nonhuman beings] gods and ghosts of the eightfold assembly of devas and nagas who resemble humans but are not human. [Unforeseen] unanticipated. [The Dharma for the unforeseen] the Dharma for preparing for sudden death (the unforeseen). Here “the unforeseen” means sudden death. Because one has cultivated pure karma beforehand, one is
born within a lotus flower and meets no hindrance or difficulty.

blocks.text: Chapter One: The Guiding Principles of Study

inline.s: The Amitabha Sutra as Spoken by the Buddha is the heart-essence that the World-Honored One spoke without being asked, the profound sutra praised by the Buddhas of all directions, the wondrous Dharma of ultimate expedience, and the most complete and sudden of guiding goals. In this sutra the World-Honored One specifically taught how to ensure rebirth in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss:
faith and vows, holding the name, single-mindedness and no confusion.
Thereby he established the
guiding principles of study
for the Pure Land school.
In the Amitabha Sutra as Spoken by the Buddha, the World-Honored One said:

“Shariputra! If there be good men or good women who hear of Amitābha Buddha and hold fast to his name, whether for one day, two days, three days, four days, five days, six days, or seven days, with single-mindedness and no confusion, then when such a person approaches the end of life, Amitābha Buddha and all the host of sages will appear before him; and when his life ends, his mind will not be inverted, and he will attain rebirth in Amitābha Buddha’s Land of Ultimate Bliss.”
Master Ouyi, the ninth patriarch of the Pure Land school, said in his Essential Explanation of the Amitabha Sutra:

“This sutra takes faith, vows, and holding the name as the cardinal essentials of practice. Without faith, vows cannot be aroused; without vows, practice cannot be guided; without the wondrous practice of holding the name, one cannot fulfill one’s vows and realize what one has believed. In the sutra, the Buddha first sets forth the dependent and principal rewards in order to arouse faith, next urges the arousing of vows in order to guide practice, and then shows the holding of the name as the direct way to reach non-retrogression. As for faith, it means believing in oneself and believing in others, believing in cause and believing in effect, believing in the phenomenal and believing in the noumenal. As for vows, they mean turning away from the Saha world and seeking the Pure Land with joy. As for practice, it means holding fast to the name, with single-mindedness and no confusion.”

Faith and vows must be given expression in diligent Buddha-recitation before they can be true faith and earnest vows. Reading Master Ouyi’s two statements together—“without the wondrous practice of holding the name, one cannot fulfill one’s vows and realize what one has believed” and “as for practice, it means holding fast to the name, with single-mindedness and no confusion”—the precise meaning is this: without the wondrous practice of holding the name with single-mindedness and no confusion, one cannot fulfill one’s vows and realize what one has believed. Therefore the resting place and concrete expression of true faith and earnest vows lie in the wondrous practice of holding the name with single-mindedness and no confusion.
Master Chewu, the twelfth patriarch of the Pure Land school, said:

“Single-mindedness and no confusion is the home of pure karma and the great gate of the Pure Land. If one has not entered this gate, in the end one is not secure. Can students of the Way fail to strive?”
(Dharma Words of Master Chewu)
In the Praise of the Pure Land and the Buddhas’ Reception Sutra, Master Xuanzang’s translation of the Amitabha Sutra, the Buddha said:

“Shariputra! If there be pure-faith good men or good women who hear of the measureless, boundless, inconceivable merit and name of the Buddha of Measureless Life and of the merits and adornments of the Land of Ultimate Bliss, and having heard, reflect upon them, whether for one day and night, or two, or three, or four, or five, or six, or seven, and hold them in mind without confusion, then when such good men or good women approach the end of life, the Buddha of Measureless Life, together with his measureless hosts of shravaka disciples and bodhisattvas, will come and stand before them, encircling them before and behind, and with compassion will aid and bless them, so that their minds are not confused. When their lives have ended, they will follow the assembly of that Buddha and be born in the pure Buddha land of the Land of Ultimate Bliss of Measureless Life. Moreover, Shariputra! Contemplating such a great matter of benefit and peace, I speak words of truth: if there be pure-faith good men or good women who hear of the inconceivable merit and name of the Buddha of Measureless Life and of the pure Buddha land of the Land of Ultimate Bliss, all of them should believe, accept, and make vows, practice as taught, and be born in that Buddha land.”

To seek birth in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss one must have true faith, earnest vows, and actual practice. Faith, vows, and practice are like a tripod standing on three legs: not one can be missing. Faith is the eye, vows are the motive power, and practice is the carrying out—the concrete realization of faith and vows. The Direct Path Within the Direct Path says:

“Faith is already firm, vows are already steadfast. Yet without actual practice to urge oneself on, faith is faith in vain and vows are vows in vain. Empty words are of no help—how could one win through by luck? Every undertaking requires bitter effort before it can succeed; how much more so the greatest matter of transcending the world!”
Therefore we students of the Pure Land school should, by the actual practice of single-mindedness and no confusion, prove our true faith and fulfill our earnest vows.
The reason Buddha-recitation must be single-minded is that “
only when there is a Mind-Only Pure Land can one be born in the Western Pure Land; it is by the purified mind of Buddha-recitation that one is responded to and born in the Western Pure Land
”—this is the principle of attaining rebirth through Buddha-recitation.
Master Yinguang said:

“Only when there is a Mind-Only Pure Land can one be born in the Western Pure Land. If one’s own mind is not pure, how can one attain rebirth at once? Even an evildoer and transgressor who attains rebirth through ten recitations of the Buddha’s name does so because the purified mind of Buddha-recitation is responded to and gives rise to the Western Pure Land.”
(Collected Writings of Master Yinguang, · Reply to Layman Qu Tianxiang’s Twenty-Seven Questions)

[Mind-Only Pure Land] The principal reward (body and mind) and the dependent reward (environment) of all living beings throughout the worlds of the ten directions differ in excellence or inferiority, purity or defilement, solely because they are transformed in response to the mind. When the mind is pure, the principal and dependent rewards that respond and transform are excellent and pure; when the mind is defiled, they are inferior and defiled. Hence the sutra says, “When the mind is pure, the land is pure”; this is what is meant by “the Mind-Only Pure Land.” Therefore the core of studying the Pure Land teaching is to purify the mind: when the mind is pure, one corresponds with the Pure Land; otherwise one corresponds with a defiled land. [Principal and dependent rewards] The principal reward is the body and mind of living beings, the true substance of the karmic retribution drawn forth by past karmic causes; hence it is called the principal reward. The dependent reward is the environment in which body and mind (the principal reward) dwell; this too is the karmic retribution drawn forth by past karmic causes, such as lands, mountains and rivers, the great earth, houses and implements, and so on.
As to why ten continuous thoughts at the time of death bring about rebirth, Master Yinguang explained:
“Though he has not personally realized single-mindedness and no confusion, his mind after all has not the least alien thought.”
(Collected Writings of Master Yinguang, Third Series, Volume Two, Letter in Reply to Layman Chen Xinru)
The original passage reads:

“In the Contemplation Sutra, when those who have committed the five heinous acts and the ten evils are about to end their lives and the marks of hell appear, a good teacher (original note: whether monk or lay, man or woman, anyone who can teach such a person to recite the Buddha’s name is called a good teacher) teaches them to recite the Buddha’s name, perhaps only ten recitations, perhaps fewer than ten; and when life ends straightaway, they too, relying on the Buddha’s compassionate power, attain rebirth carrying their karma. These ten thoughts, compared with ordinary ten thoughts, differ as heaven from an abyss in their ferocity and urgency, and so they attain rebirth. For pressed by the extreme suffering of hell, as soon as they hear the Buddha’s name they recite it with the whole of their spirit. Apart from this thought there is no other thought at all. Though he has not personally realized single-mindedness and no confusion, his mind after all has not the least alien thought.”
Master Yinguang also said:
“With a scattered mind reciting the Buddha’s name, rebirth is hard to attain. … Reciting the Buddha’s name with one mind, rebirth is certain.”
(Collected Writings of Master Yinguang, · Letter to Layman Chen Xizhou)
Master Lianchi said:
“Now that one is single-minded and unconfused, within, right mindfulness congeals; without, the Buddha is moved to come and welcome one; and casting off this karmic body, one is born in that land.”
(Commentary and Notes on the Amitabha Sutra) Take special note: “within, right mindfulness congeals; without, the Buddha is moved to come and welcome one.”
Therefore the guiding principle of study for aware Buddha-recitation is:
faith and vows, holding the name, single-mindedness and no confusion.
Question: what is meant by single-mindedness and no confusion?
Answer: compare the two translations of the Amitabha Sutra. Master Kumarajiva’s translation:
“Whether for one day, two days, three days, four days, five days, six days, or seven days, with single-mindedness and no confusion.”
Master Xuanzang’s translation:
“Whether for one day and night, or two, or three, or four, or five, or six, or seven, holding it in mind without confusion.”

Thus one knows that single-mindedness and no confusion is holding in mind without confusion. From this it can be seen that when Master Kumarajiva rendered it as “single-mindedness and no confusion,” his meaning was: reciting the Buddha’s name with one mind and one intent, not thrown into confusion by afflictions, clear and distinct throughout, neither dull nor scattered.
Question: in the passage above, does “clear and distinct throughout” mean that the Buddha’s name must be recited perfectly clearly?

Answer: that is not the meaning. “Clear and distinct throughout” means: the Buddha’s name that is recited must be clear and distinct in the mind (every phrase of the Buddha’s name is clearly known in the mind). Zhang Guangwei said:

“In the past, when I recited the Buddha’s name, I too merely mumbled it through in a blur. Only now do I know that each character must come forth from the mind, and each character must also enter back into the mind. When reciting, one should first close the eyes and sit upright, gathering the spirit and settling the thoughts, without a hair of scattered mind, restless competitiveness, or dull indolence. Opening the mouth and uttering the sound, one must let the sound issue from the mind, the mind transmit it through the mouth, the breath be regulated and the voice harmonious, neither slow nor hurried, each character distinct, each phrase continuous. Divided, a single character can be taken as one phrase; strung together, a hundred thousand phrases are as one phrase. Dense and close-woven, from one sound to a thousand myriad sounds, from one quarter hour to the twelve double hours, with no break and no continuation, nothing missing and nothing leaking away. When this becomes thoroughly familiar over a long time, the flower opens and one sees the Buddha; at that time you will verify it for yourself—it will never deceive anyone. … I wish to tell all who recite the Buddha’s name this: know that the mind must recite, and do not merely recite with the mouth. When you enter this gate, you are not far from the Buddha.”
(Remaining Words on the Pure Land)
Question: in the passage above, what is meant by “neither dull nor scattered”?

Answer: “neither dull nor scattered” means: not dull and not scattered. That is to say: if deluded thoughts arise, know them and do not follow them, and do not be thrown into confusion by deluded thoughts. So single-mindedness and no confusion in Buddha-recitation does not mean that not a single deluded thought arises; it means not being deceived and benighted by deluded thoughts (not dull) and not letting deluded thoughts continue and become thinking (not scattered). In general, it means not being thrown into confusion by deluded thoughts. Of course, this is only the most preliminary requirement of single-mindedness and no confusion; striving further on this foundation, one will reach the state in which thought after thought is free of deluded thought and the Buddha’s name is a single pure expanse.
Question: what are phenomenal single-mindedness and noumenal single-mindedness?

Answer: the full names of phenomenal single-mindedness and noumenal single-mindedness are phenomenal single-mindedness and no confusion, and noumenal single-mindedness and no confusion. The single-mindedness and no confusion spoken of above is phenomenal single-mindedness and no confusion, attained through reciting the Buddha’s name while holding it. Noumenal single-mindedness and no confusion is to be silently attuned to the unborn and to see one’s own nature clearly; it is attained through cultivating the samādhi of Buddha-recitation. Master Ouyi said:

“Phenomenal single-mindedness is to be clear and distinct throughout, neither dull nor scattered; noumenal single-mindedness is to be silently attuned to the unborn and to see one’s own nature clearly.”
(Collected Essays of Lingfeng, · Occasional Talks from the Brahma Chamber)
[Unborn] The meaning of not arising and not ceasing, that is, the principle of nirvāṇa.
Question: the sutra says:

“If there be good men or good women who hear of Amitābha Buddha and hold fast to his name, whether for one day, two days, three days, four days, five days, six days, or seven days, with single-mindedness and no confusion.”
Within those seven days, can one really attain single-mindedness and no confusion?

Answer: “whether for one day, up to seven days” is an illustrative phrase, a compressed way of speaking. The detailed way of speaking is, for example, what the World-Honored One says in the Great Discourse on the Foundations of Mindfulness:
“Monks! Anyone who cultivates the four foundations of mindfulness correctly in this way
for seven years
may expect one of two fruits: either the highest wisdom in this present life
(attaining the fruit of arhatship)
, or, if the five aggregates still remain, the fruit of non-return
(attaining the fruit of anagamin)
. Monks!
Needless to say, seven years
Monks!
Needless to say, six years
Monks!
Needless to say, one year
Monks!
Needless to say, seven months
Monks!
Needless to say, one month
Monks!
Needless to say, half a month
; if someone cultivates the four foundations of mindfulness correctly in this way
for seven days
, he may expect to obtain one of two fruits: either the highest wisdom in this present life, or, if the five aggregates still remain, the fruit of non-return.”

[Four fruits] The cultivation of the Four Noble Truths has four fruits: the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, and the fruit of arhatship. The first fruit, stream-entry (srota-apanna), is rendered in Chinese as “enter the stream,” meaning that one has just entered the stream of the sages. The second fruit, once-returning (sakridagamin), is rendered as “one return,” meaning that one who attains this fruit, after death, is reborn in the heavens as a deva for one life, and once more is born into this world of ours, and then no longer returns to the desire realm to receive birth and death. The third fruit, non-returning (anagamin), is rendered as “no return,” meaning that one who attains this fruit is no longer born in the desire realm. The fourth fruit, arhatship, is rendered as “unborn,” meaning that one who attains this fruit is liberated from birth and death, receives no further existence, and holds the highest fruit. [Desire realm] The world inhabited by living beings who have sexual desire and the desire for food.

As for the question “within seven days, can one attain single-mindedness and no confusion?” the answer is: compared with realizing the fruit of arhatship (having already cut off the delusion of views and the delusion of thought) or the fruit of non-returning (having already cut off the last nine grades of residual delusion of thought in the desire realm), single-mindedness in Buddha-recitation is truly far, far easier; so there certainly are good men and good women who can attain single-mindedness in Buddha-recitation within seven days. For instance, a practitioner who has already subdued his afflictions, once he hears how surpassing the Pure Land teaching is and therefore recites the Buddha’s name while holding it with true faith and earnest vows, can attain single-mindedness in Buddha-recitation within seven days. For one who has not subdued his afflictions, the time will be longer; how long exactly depends on each person’s foundation and progress in study. In general, so long as the method is correct (for example, practicing according to Aware Buddha-Recitation), and one adds diligent and unremitting hard effort, anyone can attain single-mindedness in Buddha-recitation within seven years. You may ask: how can this be proved? The answer is: simply do it with your feet on solid ground, and you are the proof.

Take special note: selfishness and desire most of all agitate the mind; they are the tigers in the road blocking the cultivation of single-mindedness and no confusion, and so one must cast off selfishness and be free of desire. At all times be vigilant, and do not be controlled by selfishness and desire, or the work will hardly succeed. The focus of study in the first stage of the Online Buddhist Academy of Practice According to the Teaching, “Ceasing Evil and Practicing Good,” and in the second stage, “Taking the Precepts as the Foundation,” is precisely this:
“cast off selfishness and be free of desire; purify the three karmas”

—this is the foundation of aware Buddha-recitation. (Readers who have not studied the courses of these two stages would do well to make them up in good time.) At the same time, one should become thoroughly familiar with the three essentials of mind cultivation (gathering the mind, guarding the mind, and stabilizing the mind), and constantly practice these basic skills.

[Three karmas] The karma of the body, the karma of the mouth, and the karma of the mind. [Purify the three karmas] Purifying the karma of the body: not killing, not stealing, not committing sexual misconduct. Purifying the karma of the mouth: not lying, not speaking divisively, not speaking harshly, not speaking idly. Purifying the karma of the mind: not being greedy, not being angry, not being deluded. [Gathering the mind, guarding the mind, and stabilizing the mind] Gathering the mind is to gather back the mind that has been lost. Guarding the mind is to guard firmly the mind that has been gathered back. Stabilizing the mind is, at the very moment when the mind is about to be lost but is not yet lost, to stabilize it and hold it unmoving—like pulling a horse back at the edge of a cliff.

In cultivation one must train hard and train skillfully. Training hard is to climb on without fearing hardship; training skillfully is to be good at finding the path. So long as all the power of the mind is focused on cultivating single-mindedness and no confusion, creative methods will arise in response and one must catch them in time. Then, following the optimizing cycle of “practice, review, improve (draw up a new plan); practice again, review again, improve again (draw up a new plan),” one goes ever deeper and higher, and forms a set of methods most effective for oneself.

At all times examine yourself: am I giving my all? Is all the power of my mind focused on cultivating single-mindedness and no confusion? Am I at every moment pondering, reviewing, trying, and persisting? This is like drilling wood to make fire: first, the method must be correct; second, one must drill unremittingly. Method is indeed very important, but even with a correct method, if one drills a while and then stops, one will never drill out fire. Therefore one who recites the Buddha’s name must have true faith and earnest vows, and be diligent without slackening. Though a whole life of hardship is but a moment, once you reach the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss, your lifespan is measureless and your joy without limit; you accomplish Buddhahood, save living beings, and fulfill the great bodhi vow.
Question: since Buddha-recitation must reach single-mindedness and no confusion, why is the Pure Land teaching still called the easy path?

Answer: there are two kinds of path for escaping the cycle of birth and death: the common path and the Pure Land path. On the common path one must cut off the afflictions of view and thought entirely before one can escape the cycle of birth and death, and this is extremely difficult. On the Pure Land path one need only attain single-mindedness in Buddha-recitation (using the Buddha’s name to subdue the afflictions), and at the time of death one attains rebirth in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss, escaping the cycle of birth and death; this is far, far easier than cutting off the afflictions of view and thought. Moreover, so long as the method is correct and one works hard, single-mindedness in Buddha-recitation is something anyone can attain. Hence the Pure Land teaching is called the easy path.

blocks.text: Chapter Two: The Three Blessings of Pure Karma

inline.s: In the Amitabha Sutra as Spoken by the Buddha, the Buddha says:
“One cannot be born in that land
(the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss)
with few roots of goodness and blessings and causal conditions.”
In the Contemplation Sutra of the Buddha of Measureless Life, the Buddha says:

“Those who wish to be born in that land should cultivate three blessings. First, to care for and nourish one’s parents, to serve and attend one’s teachers, to have a compassionate mind and not kill, and to cultivate the ten good karmas. Second, to receive and uphold the three refuges, to fulfill all the precepts, and not to violate the deportment. Third, to give rise to the bodhi mind, to deeply believe in cause and effect, to read and recite the Mahayana scriptures, and to encourage others to advance. These three matters are called pure karma.” “Do you now know? These three kinds of karma are the true cause of pure karma for all Buddhas of the past, future, and present.”

Therefore one who recites the Buddha’s name must observe and cultivate the three blessings of pure karma, so as to possess the causal conditions of abundant roots of goodness and blessings; this is the foundation of study in the Pure Land school.

[Roots of goodness] The goodness of the three karmas of body, mouth, and mind; because it can produce wondrous fruits, it is called a root of goodness. [Ten good karmas] The ten kinds of good karma: not killing, not stealing, not committing sexual misconduct, not lying, not speaking divisively (not stirring up trouble between people), not speaking harshly (not mocking with an evil sound), not speaking idly (not speaking meaningless words), not being greedy, not being angry, and not being deluded (not going against reason). [Three refuges] The three refuges (threefold refuge): taking refuge in the Buddha, taking refuge in the Dharma, taking refuge in the Sangha. This is taking refuge in the Three Jewels: all Buddhas are the Buddha Jewel, the right Dharma is the Dharma Jewel, and the sages of the Sangha are the Sangha Jewel. [Giving rise to the bodhi mind] Arousing the great mind that seeks the Buddha Way above (to become a Buddha) and transforms living beings below.

In the first stage, “Ceasing Evil and Practicing Good,” the courses of study are the Original Vows Sutra of Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva, Liaofan’s Four Lessons, The Record of Mr. Yu Jingyi Meeting the Kitchen God, The Auspicious Words of Wang Fengyi, and the Treatise on Response and Retribution; the core of study is
“care for and nourish one’s parents, serve and attend one’s teachers, have a compassionate mind and not kill, and cultivate the ten good karmas

In the second stage, “Taking the Precepts as the Foundation,” the courses of study are the Sutra of Forty-Two Chapters, the Sutra of the Eight Realizations of the Great Beings, the Sutra of the Buddha’s Bequeathed Teaching, the Sutra on the Ten Good Karma Paths, and the Great Discourse on the Foundations of Mindfulness; the core of study is
“receive and uphold the three refuges, fulfill all the precepts, and not violate the deportment

In the third stage, “Prajnā Smashing Delusion,” the courses of study are the Diamond Sutra, the Heart Sutra, the Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch, the Sutra of the Buddha’s Treasury, and A Direct Explanation of the True Mind; the core of study is
“give rise to the bodhi mind, deeply believe in cause and effect, read and recite the Mahayana scriptures, and encourage others to advance

In the fourth stage, “Returning to the Pure Land,” the courses of study are the Praise of the Pure Land and the Buddhas’ Reception Sutra, A Treatise on Buddha-Recitation, The Essentials of Chan and Pure Land, the Perfect Penetration Chapter of Great Strength Bodhisattva, and In Search of the Elephant of Buddha-Recitation Samādhi; the core of study is
“faith and vows, holding the name, single-mindedness and no confusion

Studying these courses both gathers the provisions for rebirth in the Pure Land and clears away the hindrances and difficulties on the road ahead; they are the foundation of “aware Buddha-recitation,” and must be studied solidly and well. Purifying offenses and gathering provisions (clearing away karmic hindrances and gathering provisions) is a most important aspect of study in the Pure Land school; one must truly apply effort and bring knowledge and action into one.

[Provisions] Zi means resources, liang means grain. Cultivating the Way is like a long journey: one needs provisions to sustain oneself before one can reach the destination. Faith, vows, and practice are the provisions for rebirth in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss, and are often called the three provisions of the Pure Land.
In the Praise of the Pure Land and the Buddhas’ Reception Sutra, the World-Honored One taught:
“All you sentient beings should believe and accept this praise of the inconceivable merits of the Buddha land, the
Dharma gate
of the reception of all Buddhas.”

Therefore Buddha-recitation seeking rebirth in the Pure Land is the Dharma gate by which all Buddhas receive and embrace beings, and moreover in this sutra the World-Honored One clearly and specifically taught how to practice this Dharma gate.
After the World-Honored One had spoken

“If there be pure-faith good men or good women who hear of the measureless, boundless, inconceivable merit and name of the Buddha of Measureless Life and the merits and adornments of the Land of Ultimate Bliss;
having heard, reflect upon them
, whether for one day and night, or two, or three, or four, or five, or six, or seven,
holding them in mind without confusion

. When such good men or good women approach the end of life, the Buddha of Measureless Life, together with his measureless hosts of shravaka disciples and bodhisattvas, will come and stand before them, encircling them before and behind, and with compassion will aid and bless them, so that their minds are not confused. When their lives have ended, they will follow the assembly of that Buddha and be born in the pure Buddha land of the Land of Ultimate Bliss of Measureless Life”
, he immediately said:

“If there be pure-faith good men or good women who hear of the inconceivable merit and name of the Buddha of Measureless Life and of the pure Buddha land of the Land of Ultimate Bliss, all of them should
believe, accept, and make vows, practice as taught, and be born in that Buddha land.

Here the World-Honored One set out faith, vows, and practice with perfect clarity: faith is to “believe and accept”; vows are to “make vows”; practice is to “practice as taught”—holding in mind without confusion (single-mindedness and no confusion).

While faith and vows remain merely in the head, they are no more than an idea. Faith and vows must be put into practice; only then are they true faith and steadfast vows. Therefore true faith and steadfast vows necessarily lead to vigorous practice. Without genuine and diligent practice, how can one realize what one believes? How can one fulfill one’s vows? Faith and vows without vigorous practice are merely empty faith and floating vows.

In this sutra the World-Honored One again and again, over and over, stressed “practice as taught,” and told us plainly: so long as one practices as taught, one is received and embraced by all the Buddhas of the ten directions, one will certainly be born in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss, one will never fall back but will quickly realize the Buddha fruit. His care shines through his words. The World-Honored One taught:

“If there be pure-faith good men or good women who hear of the inconceivable merit and name of the Buddha of Measureless Life and of the pure Buddha land of the Land of Ultimate Bliss, all of them should believe, accept, and make vows,
practice as taught
, and be born in that Buddha land.”
Those who practice as taught

will all certainly attain non-retrogression in the supreme perfect enlightenment, and will all certainly be born in the pure Buddha land of the Land of Ultimate Bliss of the Buddha of Measureless Life. Therefore, Shariputra, all you sentient beings should
believe, accept, and comprehend the words of myself and of the Buddhas and World-Honored Ones of the ten directions
, and should strive diligently,
practicing as taught
, without giving rise to doubt.”
Those who practice as taught

will all certainly attain non-retrogression in the supreme perfect enlightenment, and will all certainly be born in the pure Buddha land of the Land of Ultimate Bliss of the Buddha of Measureless Life. Therefore, Shariputra, if there be pure-faith good men or good women, all of them should deeply believe and understand the pure Buddha land of the Land of Ultimate Bliss of Measureless Life, make vows to be born there,
and not act heedlessly

“In this defiled and forbearance-enduring world, in this evil age of the five turbidities, if there be pure-faith good men or good women who hear this Dharma, so extremely hard to believe in all the world, and can give rise to faith and understanding, receive, uphold, and expound it,
and practice according to the teaching

, know that such a person is most rare, and has planted roots of goodness in the presence of measureless Buddhas. When such a person’s life ends, he will certainly be born in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss, and enjoy the great Mahayana joy of the pure Buddha land adorned with all kinds of merits.”
Therefore students must deeply believe and understand the meaning of “practice as taught” and put it into action, pressing forward daily without looking back. The Vimalakirti Sutra says:
“If one wishes to attain the Pure Land, one should purify one’s mind; as one’s mind becomes pure, the Buddha land is pure.”

The minds of living beings are like water, and Amitābha Buddha is like the moon. When the water of the mind is clear and still and corresponds with the Pure Land (the Land of Ultimate Bliss), the Buddha-moon appears before one; when the water of the mind is turbid and disordered and corresponds with a defiled land (the Saha world), the Buddha-moon does not show. Therefore the Dharma gate of Buddha-recitation is to gather in all six faculties and let pure mindfulness continue without interruption, so that the turbid and disordered water of the mind becomes clear and still (single-mindedness and no confusion), and one goes on to remove the mud and keep only the water (the samādhi of Buddha-recitation).

The guiding principle of study for aware Buddha-recitation is: true faith and earnest vows, single-mindedness and no confusion. Because of true faith, the eye clearly perceives what lies before it, and one sees the goal and the road perfectly clearly; because of earnest vows, the motive power is matchless, like a river bursting its banks, rushing on with nothing able to withstand it. With true faith and earnest vows, one will certainly follow the World-Honored One’s earnest teaching to “practice as taught,” and so bring about the wondrous practice of single-mindedness and no confusion, and by that wondrous practice prove what one believes and fulfill one’s vows:
“Now that one is single-minded and unconfused,
(at the time of death)
within, right mindfulness congeals; without, the Buddha is moved to come and welcome one; and casting off this karmic body, one is born in that land.”
(Master Lianchi, Commentary and Notes on the Amitabha Sutra)
[Rushing on with nothing able to withstand it] Surging and vast, with nothing whatsoever able to resist it.
On the relationship among true faith, earnest vows, and steadfast practice, Master Chewu (the twelfth patriarch of the Pure Land school) taught:
“Let those without faith be set aside for the moment
(as for those without faith, let us set them aside and say no more of them)

. Even among those who have faith, if one has faith but no vows, it is as though one had no faith. If one has vows but no practice, it is as though one had no vows. If one practices but not fiercely, it is as though one did not practice. The reason practice is not fierce is that the vows are not earnest. The reason the vows are not earnest is that the faith is not true. In short, it is hard to give rise to true faith. If faith is truly there, the vows will of themselves be earnest. If the vows are truly earnest, the practice will of itself be fierce. With true and earnest faith and vows, together with brave and vigorous practice, one will certainly attain rebirth in the Pure Land, certainly see Amitābha Buddha, certainly realize the three kinds of non-retrogression, and certainly in one life become a Buddha.”

(Bequeathed Collected Works of Master Chewu) Therefore whether one’s faith and vows are true and earnest is tested by whether one’s practice is fierce. No practice, or practice that is not fierce, shows that the faith is empty and the vows are floating.

Single-mindedness and no confusion (holding in mind without confusion) is what Great Strength Bodhisattva called “pure mindfulness continuing without interruption,” and also what Master Shandao (the second patriarch of the Pure Land school) called “thought following thought without a break.” Master Shandao said:
“Therefore the Great Sage
(Shakyamuni Buddha)

, in his compassion, directly urged us to recite the name exclusively; precisely because reciting the name is easy, continued recitation brings rebirth. If one can make thought follow thought without a break, with one’s whole life as the term, then ten out of ten are born, a hundred out of a hundred are born. … May all people reflect well on this: in walking, standing, sitting, and lying down, one must rouse the mind and master oneself, and never let up day or night; the former thought ends at death and the next thought is born at once, forever enjoying the joy of the unconditioned Dharma, until one becomes a Buddha—is this not wonderful!”

(Quoted from The Essentials of Buddha-Recitation) Therefore, to have thought follow thought without a break in daily life is the guarantee of right mindfulness being clear at the time of death; and right mindfulness being clear at the time of death is in turn the key to rebirth in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss.
Master Shandao, in his Essay on Right Mindfulness at the Time of Death, says:

“The son who knows his home asked: among the great matters of the world, none surpasses birth and death. If one breath does not return, one belongs to the next life; if one thought goes astray, one falls into the cycle of rebirth. I have repeatedly received your instruction on the method of Buddha-recitation and rebirth, and its principle is perfectly clear. Yet I fear that when sickness comes and death approaches, my mind and consciousness will be scattered, and I further fear that others may disturb my right mindfulness and make me lose the pure cause. I beg you to show again the way home, so that I may escape the suffering of sinking down. The master said: A good question! Anyone who wishes to be born in the Pure Land at the end of life must not fear death. Constantly remember that this body has much suffering, and that impure evil karma entangles one in every way. If one can cast off this defiled body and be born beyond into the Pure Land, receiving measureless joy and being liberated from the bitter course of birth and death, that is a matter to one’s liking, like taking off a worn-out garment and being given precious robes. One should simply let go of body and mind and not cling to them. … If the illness is grave and death is near, relatives must not shed tears and weep, nor utter sighs of grief and regret, disturbing the mind and spirit and making one lose right mindfulness. They should only recite the Buddha’s name together in one voice, and may weep only after the breath has ceased. The least thought clinging to the world becomes a hindrance, and one is not liberated. … I have often seen people who in ordinary times recite the Buddha’s name, bow, and praise, and vow to seek rebirth in the West, most earnestly and sincerely
(fervently and truly)

. Yet when illness comes, they fear death, and speak not at all of rebirth and liberation. Only when the breath has stopped and life is over, and consciousness enters the dark realm, do they begin their ten recitations. That is like shutting the gate after the thief has gone—what use is it? Birth and death are a great matter, and one must apply one’s own effort. If one thought goes astray, one suffers for kalpas—who can take one’s place? Think on this, think on this!”
(Quoted from Longshu’s Essays on the Pure Land)

blocks.text: Chapter Four: Aware of the Buddha’s Name

inline.s: The key to reciting the Buddha’s name well is to have a powerful power of mindfulness—focused, continuous, and lasting—with all three hundred and sixty joints and eighty-four thousand pores of the whole body focused on the Buddha’s name, reciting with the whole body and mind. As the saying goes: when two armies meet, the brave one wins. One who recites the Buddha’s name must conquer karma and deluded thought with a powerful power of mindfulness. To recite well, the power of mindfulness is crucial, and the strength of that power comes from faith and vows. By the strength or weakness of your power of mindfulness you should examine whether your faith and vows are true and earnest, and so know how to improve.
[Power of mindfulness] The power of focused mindfulness, able to withstand interference and temptation. The Sutra of the Buddha’s Bequeathed Teaching says:
“If the power of mindfulness is firm and strong, then even though one enters among the robbers of the five desires, one is not harmed by them.”
The Sutra of the Practice of Contemplating Samantabhadra Bodhisattva as Spoken by the Buddha says:
“Because the power of mindfulness is strong, one may see my body.”

[Five desires] The desires for form, sound, fragrance, taste, and touch. Form means beautiful appearances; sound means pleasing sounds and delightful words; fragrance means fragrant scents; taste means delicious flavors; touch means agreeable tactile pleasure. Because these five can cause people to give rise to a mind of greed, they are called the five desires.

The task of this stage is to be aware of the Buddha’s name: to know it as you recite it. The method is to recite character by character: Na—, Mo—, A—, Mi—, Tuo—, Fo—, aware of each character. This is an expedient for beginners; once the practice is well in hand, one may gradually shorten the interval between characters, until the phrases of the Buddha’s name come densely and continuously, like breathing. Practice this way for a long time, and the Buddha’s name will of itself pour forth in the mind in an unbroken stream and become the main melody of one’s life; add to this awareness of each character, and the Buddha’s name will be “clear and distinct throughout, neither dull nor scattered.”

Another method is breath-based Buddha-recitation: with each out-breath (each exhalation) silently recite one character, aware of each character. (Of course, one may also silently recite one character with each in-breath, or one character per breath, or several characters per breath. In short, follow each person’s habit, so long as it gathers in the mind and lasts.) This is the Precious King’s method of following the breath. Master Feixi of the Tang dynasty says in his Treatise on the Precious King of Buddha-Recitation Samādhi:

“People in the world mostly use precious jade, crystal, diamond, bodhi seeds, or wooden beads as their counting beads. I, however, take the in- and out-breath as my counting beads. I recite the Buddha’s name, following it with the breath; I have a great reliance—why should I fear that when one breath does not return
(when a single breath fails)

I shall belong to the next life? In walking, standing, sitting, and lying down I constantly use these beads. Even if dull and drowsy, I fall asleep still holding the Buddha in my mouth, and on waking I continue. Thus in dreams I shall surely see that Buddha. It is like drilling wood: when smoke flies up, it is the forerunner of fire. If one does not stop dreaming of him, the samādhi is accomplished. To behold the jade-like mark of his brow and personally receive his prediction—of this there is no shadow of doubt.”
For more information on breath-based Buddha-recitation, see the essay
The Essentials of Breath-Based Buddha-Recitation

[Like drilling wood: when smoke flies up, it is the forerunner of fire] As when drilling wood to make fire, if smoke comes out, one knows that fire will soon arise. Smoke flying up is the sign that fire is about to start; here it is used to illustrate that seeing the Buddha in dreams is the sign that the samādhi of Buddha-recitation is about to be accomplished. [Drilling the fire-drill (sui)] Also written with a different character. Drilling the fire-drill to make fire is the most primitive method of making fire; the drill is the tool for taking fire.
Each person may also choose the method of Buddha-recitation that suits him best; the key is to be aware of each character, and never let the mouth run on emptily while the mind is elsewhere.
On this point,
Master Lianchi, the eighth patriarch of the Pure Land school, said:
“To recollect and recite means: hearing the Buddha’s name, constantly remembering and constantly reciting it,
traversing it with the mind, each character distinct

, the former phrase and the latter phrase continuing without a break, in walking, standing, sitting, and lying down only this one thought and no second thought, not thrown into confusion by thoughts of greed, anger, and affliction. This is what the Sutra of the Accomplished Light Samādhi means by ‘in leisure and solitude, single the mind; amid the crowd of afflictions, single the mind; even amid praise and slander, gain and loss, good and evil, in all such places, single the mind.’”
(Dharma Collection of Yunqi) Take special note:
“traversing it with the mind, each character distinct.”
This is awareness of each character.
Master Chewu, the twelfth patriarch of the Pure Land school, taught:
“What is called holding fast to the name is simply earnest and unwavering adherence
(firmly engraving it in the mind)

, that is, holding it firmly in the mind without a moment’s forgetting. If even one thought is interrupted, it is not holding fast. If even one thought is mixed in, it is not holding fast. Thought following thought without a break, without mixture and without interval—this is true diligence. With unceasing diligence, one gradually enters single-mindedness and no confusion, and brings pure karma to perfection.”
(Bequeathed Collected Works of Master Chewu)
[Earnest and unwavering adherence (
yīng

)] “Earnest” means holding fast without letting go, extended to mean fervent; “adherence” means engraving in the mind. “Earnest and unwavering adherence” describes remembering fervently and never forgetting.

In aware Buddha-recitation, walking meditation is very important; one should walk and recite as much as possible, and after long practice one will of oneself understand its subtle wonder. Master Yongming said:
“Question: the treatise asks, how do the merits of reciting while walking
(walking meditation)

and reciting while sitting compare? Answer: it is like setting sail against the current—even then one may be said to make progress; how much faster when one sets sail with the current. A single recitation while sitting still dissolves the offenses of eighty million kalpas; who can know the measure of the merit of reciting while walking? Hence the verse: walk the path five hundred times, recite the Buddha’s name a thousand times; if one’s work is always like this, the West and the Buddha will come of themselves.”
(Quoted from The Essentials of Buddha-Recitation)

[Walk the path five hundred times, recite the Buddha’s name a thousand times] “Walking the path” means walking meditation, and also refers to ordinary walking (going on foot). The method of “walking the path five hundred times, reciting the Buddha’s name a thousand times” is: one step, one recitation of the Buddha’s name; two steps (right step, left step) make one round.

At the beginning, the method of walking and reciting is: one step, one character, aware of each step and each character. If one walks in a circle, then with each circuit (or at a fixed check-point of one’s own choosing) check once: have I fallen into deluded thought? Then raise awareness and recite earnestly. If one walks back and forth, then after each turn pause for a moment and check whether deluded thoughts have arisen. When the walking is finished, reflect on how the recitation went, gather the lessons and the insights, and decide clearly what to do next time. Once walking and reciting have become proficient, with awareness of each character, one may recite two characters per step, or one whole phrase per step.

At ordinary times one must maintain awareness and strive to keep it unbroken. Before the skill of single-mindedness and no confusion is accomplished, the most important task is this: closely monitor whether one has fallen into deluded thought. When you notice it, raise the Buddha’s name at once, be aware of each character, and come out of the world of deluded thought. Do the work densely and meticulously; the key lies in persisting and holding to it. When the practice is deep, then you will grasp the wonder of the patriarchs’ teaching:

“One who recites the Buddha’s name must have earnest faith and a stern sense of the true cause. Let him deeply ponder the sorrow of birth and death and the turning of the wheel, and deeply loathe the pain of the dust of toil and its confusion. Raise one recitation of the Buddha’s name, and straightaway let there be no other view. Like the Tai’e sword laid across the hall; like a great fire-wheel, leaping with blazing flame. Whatever meets it is scorched, whatever touches it is wounded. Straight on until single-mindedness and no confusion, with subject and object both forgotten.”
(Zhongfeng’s Three Sessions of Recitation)

“When Amitābha Buddha is recited until one is thoroughly familiar with him, the ultimate doctrine of the twelve divisions of the three baskets is all in it; the upward mechanism of the seventeen hundred koans is also in it; the three thousand deportments, the eighty thousand fine practices, and the three categories of pure precepts are also in it. Truly able to recite the Buddha’s name, one lets go of body, mind, and world—this is great giving. Truly able to recite the Buddha’s name, one no longer gives rise to greed, anger, and delusion—this is great precept-keeping. Truly able to recite the Buddha’s name, one does not reckon right and wrong, self and other—this is great patience. Truly able to recite the Buddha’s name, one lets not the slightest interval or mixture occur—this is great diligence. Truly able to recite the Buddha’s name, one no longer chases after deluded thoughts—this is great samādhi. Truly able to recite the Buddha’s name, one is not deluded by other byways—this is great wisdom.”
(Master Ouyi, Instructions on the Dharma Gate of Buddha-Recitation)
Question: to be aware of each character in Buddha-recitation is quite taxing, and deluded thoughts keep arising without stopping. What should I do?

Answer: if that is so, you may place your attention on the changes in the shape of the mouth and be aware of each character. Once the practice is well in hand, you may discard this walking stick. If even this does not work, it shows that your power of awareness is too weak; you must strengthen your study of the “preliminary” stage in order to cultivate a focused, continuous, and lasting power of awareness. Lay the foundation solidly first, and then advance once it is full.
Question: I have practiced breath-based Buddha-recitation for several years, but I cannot control my deluded thoughts. What should I do?

Answer: in the beginning stages of breath-based Buddha-recitation, following the breath (letting the mind go along with the breath) serves as a walking stick. When reciting in this way, one must be aware of the breath. When the practice matures and the mind gradually gathers, then one no longer pays attention to the breath but focuses on the thought of reciting the Buddha’s name. Of course, if following the breath already gathers the mind in well, one may continue with this method.

Alternatively, one may practice breath-based Buddha-recitation in this way: abdominal breathing, with the belly bulging outward on the in-breath and sinking inward on the out-breath. The breathing must be natural—this point is very important. When first practicing, one may place a hand on the belly and feel its rising and falling. As the belly bulges outward (in-breath), recite “A Mi”; as it sinks inward (out-breath), recite “Tuo Fo.” In the beginning stage, while reciting, one should be aware of the bulging and sinking of the belly, using this as a walking stick. When the practice matures and the mind gradually gathers, then one no longer attends to the bulging and sinking of the belly but focuses on the thought of reciting the Buddha’s name.

In Buddha-recitation, what is most to be avoided is drifting without a home—reciting and reciting until one is swept away by deluded thoughts and no longer knows what one is saying. So in the beginning stage one should add the ten-breath counting method to breath-based Buddha-recitation to help stop deluded thoughts: count once with each breath, counting from one to ten (

; bend the little finger at five, straighten it at six), and then count from one to ten again, over and over in a cycle. In counting, use the bending and straightening of the fingers of one hand: with the left hand (the right may also be used), bend one finger with each breath, and when all five are bent, straighten one finger with each breath; when all five are straight again, ten breaths have been taken.

Counting by the bending and straightening of the fingers is very important; in time you will come to understand its subtle wonder. When the practice is deep, one no longer counts, and at that point there are no deluded thoughts either.

The ten-breath counting method has another advantage: each time you reach ten, check how those ten breaths of recitation went. Discover problems in good time and solve them in good time. Then, mentally prepared, rouse your spirits and recite the next ten breaths well. With such immediate feedback and immediate handling, it seems to cost time and effort at first, but once familiar it becomes effortless, and the more one recites the purer and finer it becomes. Persisting in this way, one can attain single-mindedness and no confusion with full confidence.

To make the practice of breath-based Buddha-recitation even more meticulous, one may also breathe slowly with the abdomen, and with every breath know clearly in the mind: within this breath, are there deluded thoughts or not?
On breath-based Buddha-recitation, Master Tanxu taught:
“There is also a most convenient method: breath-based Buddha-recitation. As you breathe in
(inhalation)

, recite ‘Namo Ami’; as you breathe out, recite ‘Tuo Fo.’ In this way, so long as a person has a breath, he recites the Buddha’s name once; and in time, at every moment, in walking, standing, sitting, and lying down, he does not depart from one recitation of Amitābha Buddha. This is true diligence. When a person is at the end of life and the last breath is about to stop, the karma of a whole lifetime follows that last breath of Buddha-recitation, and he is born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss and sees Amitābha Buddha.”
The Master also taught:

“The practitioner sits upright with the body straight, regulates the breathing so that it is neither too fast nor too slow, neither rough nor gasping, but calm and slow with each in- and out-breath. Then he recites according to the breath, using either the four-character or the six-character form, though the four-character form is better. He divides the Buddha’s name into two beats, reciting ‘A Mi’ on the out-breath and ‘Tuo Fo’ on the in-breath
But he must use abdominal breathing, attending to the lower abdomen and letting it be natural.

This method may be used in rest, in sleep, in sitting, and in standing. If practiced long until thoroughly familiar, right mindfulness is not lost, and when the breath stops one is at once born in the West.
It is a supreme method of reciting the name while holding it
, and those with the aspiration for the West should take note of it.”
